What's Written Down About Your Wife's Day, Who Knows the Rest, and Who Has a Copy

A one-page record of where each piece of her day lives, on paper or in someone's head, and who on the new team has been given what.

Download PDF

Her mornings are in your head. Her evenings are in your daughter's. The dietary instructions from the doctor's office are in a folder somewhere in the kitchen.

This page doesn't ask you to write any of it out. It asks where each piece lives, how recent it is, and who on the new team has been handed a copy.

What's still only in someone's head, and who will write it down

Anything above with nothing in the second column. Put a name next to each.

For example Her evenings. Our daughter knows them better than I do. She'll write them out on Thursday.

How to use it

  • Don't copy her routines onto this page. Just say where each one is written, or who carries it.
  • Next to anything written down, note the date and whose words they are: hers, yours or someone else's.
  • For the allergy and dietary papers, note who gave them and the date printed on them. Don't restate them in your own words.
  • Bring this page along with the short page about her on the first day.

What this page doesn't do

It doesn't explain what any written instruction means or say which of her preferences matters most. If something in the instructions is unclear, that's a question for the clinician who wrote it.
